clue.text: Switch edges on dresses? That's rational

indicators.note: the edges of a word are its first and last letters, and switching them trades their places while the middle stays put

parts.note: robes are long loose garments, so dresses as a plural noun

explanation.surface: Someone tidying the hems of their frocks and congratulating themselves on being so sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the outer letters move: ROBES keeps OBE in the middle and swaps R and S to give SOBER.
explanation.definitionFit: Sober means clear-headed and level, which is a standard synonym for reasonable or sensible thinking.

clue.text: A place to go after hidden traitors

definitions.note: loosely: spies who work covertly against a side

indicators.note: coming after places one piece directly behind the other, fixing the order of the parts

parts.note: something hidden is kept secret
taken as written
the gents is a men's public toilet, a place to go when nature calls

explanation.surface: A hideout or destination for chasing down concealed turncoats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go after' reads as chase, but 'go' belongs to the toilet euphemism and 'after' only orders the pieces. The gents is British slang for a men's lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: Spies who pass information covertly to an enemy betray their own side, so the setter treats them as turncoats.

clue.text: Truncheon William shortened, adding wedge perhaps

indicators.note: to add is to attach more on the end, so a second piece follows the first

parts.note: Billy is a familiar short form of the name William
a wedge is a golf club used for lofted shots; 'perhaps' marks it as one example

explanation.surface: A policeman named William trims his baton and fixes a wedge to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortened' does not delete letters here; it points to the pet name, as Bill or Billy is the short form of William.
explanation.definitionFit: A billy club is the American term for a police officer's wooden baton, the same weapon as a British policeman's stick.

clue.text: Rescind brief authority

definitions.meaning: first meaning: as a verb, to cancel or refrain from exacting a debt or penalty
second meaning: as a noun, the area of responsibility given to someone

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as cancelling a short-lived mandate; the verb and the noun are separate senses, the noun stressed on its first syllable in British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A remit is the task and scope of powers handed to a committee or official, while to remit a fine is to cancel it.

clue.text: Ambition to have job that's upright

parts.note: a goal is an aim or ambition
a post is a position of employment

explanation.surface: Someone hoping to land an honest, morally upright position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright' pretends to describe a decent job; it is the noun for a vertical bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the two vertical poles that frame a goal in football or rugby is called an upright.

clue.text: Tailor (tiny and agile) creates warm atmosphere

indicators.note: a tailor cuts and alters material into a new shape, so the letters are refashioned

parts.note: the letters of these words, without 'and', are the raw material

explanation.surface: A small, nimble tailor whose friendly manner makes the shop a cosy place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailor' looks like the subject of the sentence but is a verb telling you to rework the letters; 'and' in the brackets is not part of the material.
explanation.definitionFit: Geniality is friendly cheerfulness, and a gathering full of it has a cordial, welcoming feel.

clue.text: With skill, you can take odd bits off fat belly

indicators.note: removing the characters in odd-numbered places leaves only those in even positions

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters are kept

explanation.surface: Diet advice: done properly, you can trim bits off a paunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd bits' sounds like scraps of flesh; it means letters 1, 3, 5 and 7, leaving the even letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ably is the adverb from able, describing something done competently and well.

clue.text: Strong face lacks depth but shows some promise

parts.note: potent means powerful or strong

indicators.note: to lack something is to be without it, so one letter is dropped

parts.note: a dial is a clock face, and also slang for a person's face
D is the abbreviation for depth

explanation.surface: A determined-looking face that isn't deep yet hints at future talent.
explanation.walkthrough: Face as a clock face is the crossword's favourite trick; depth is the standard D, and only that letter is lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Potential is the noun for latent capacity that may develop, just as showing promise means showing future ability.

clue.text: Find fault with shot when the temperature drops dramatically

indicators.note: a sharp fall in temperature swaps a warm word for its chilly opposite inside the word

parts.note: taken as written, read as S plus a word for warm

explanation.surface: Blaming a missed shot on a sudden cold snap.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the word as S-HOT; when hot plunges to cold, S-HOT becomes S-COLD.
explanation.definitionFit: To scold is to rebuke or criticise someone angrily, which is to tell them off for their faults.

clue.text: In no time, a local concocted soothing medicine

indicators.note: to concoct is to mix up ingredients into something new

parts.note: every letter of these words is the material

explanation.surface: A villager quickly mixes up a home remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In no time' looks like a time phrase and 'a local' like a person, but all fourteen letters go into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Calamine is a pink zinc-based preparation dabbed on sunburn, insect bites and itchy rashes to calm the skin.

clue.text: Iron-based swings sound like suitable fairground attractions

indicators.note: sounding like something means matching it when spoken, not when written

parts.note: ferrous means containing iron, and to wheel is to swing round in a curve

explanation.surface: Playground swings made of iron would suit a funfair.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that iron wheels would indeed suit the ride; the first word is named after its inventor, George Ferris, not iron.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant revolving upright wheels carrying passenger cars are classic rides at funfairs and amusement parks.

clue.text: For example, add young parsnip tips to dish from north Africa?

definitions.note: an adjective; one specific example of a North African origin

parts.note: e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, meaning for example

indicators.note: the tips of words are their extreme ends, here their opening letters

parts.note: the first letter of each word
a tian is a Provençal baked vegetable dish, named after its earthenware pot

explanation.surface: A recipe tip: add baby parsnips to a North African dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is by example: Egypt is one country in north Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Egypt lies in the north-east corner of the continent, so anything Egyptian comes from that part of the world.

clue.text: Stressed from being off centre? Au contraire!

indicators.note: French for on the contrary, so each word is replaced by its opposite

parts.note: the opposite of off
the edge is the opposite of the centre

explanation.surface: Someone complaining that their nerves come from feeling off balance.
explanation.walkthrough: Reverse the sense of both words in 'off centre' and you reach the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on edge is an idiom for feeling tense, nervous and irritable, the state of someone under pressure.

clue.text: Big band playing around Long Island, performing without rehearsal

indicators.note: to go around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another
musicians playing improvise and rearrange, so the letters move freely

parts.note: the letters of these words are the material
LI is the standard abbreviation for Long Island, New York

explanation.surface: A swing orchestra touring Long Island, improvising its set on the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big band' looks like the subject doing the playing, but its seven letters are the material, rearranged so they can enclose the island.
explanation.definitionFit: To ad-lib is to improvise lines or music on the spot, from the Latin ad libitum, at pleasure.

clue.text: We blogged about having slight limb deformity

indicators.note: to move about is to wander in all directions, so the letters are scattered

parts.note: every letter of these words is the material

explanation.surface: Bloggers writing posts about their own slightly crooked legs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'on the subject of', but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowlegged describes legs that curve outwards at the knee, a mild bowing deformity of the lower limbs.

clue.text: Cluster of small pellets thrown at gophers

indicators.note: things thrown get scattered and land in a jumbled order

parts.note: every letter of these words is the material

explanation.surface: Someone hurling buckshot at burrowing rodents in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrown' fits the picture of pellets being fired, which hides its job as the rearranging signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Grapeshot was old cannon ammunition: a mass of small iron balls packed together like a bunch of grapes.

clue.text: Pick up hot dog

parts.note: both mean fashionable or popular
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A street-food order: grab a frankfurter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot dog' reads as the sausage snack; split it into two separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur a cost or penalty is to acquire it or bring it on oneself, as one might pick up a fine.

clue.text: Roman team leader's small change with first game coming up

parts.note: a cent is a coin of small value

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means reading from the bottom upwards

parts.note: first is number one, written No. I
RU is Rugby Union

explanation.surface: A Roman sports captain counting loose coins before the opening match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Team leader' sounds sporting, but a centurion commanded a century, a unit of about a hundred Roman soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A centurion was the officer in charge of a century in the Roman army, so the head of a fighting unit.

clue.text: Joint that with added grease helps hard work

parts.note: surface reading: a stiff joint that works better once oiled
setter's reading: adding grease to this arm joint gives the idiom for strenuous physical effort

explanation.surface: A creaky knee or hip that, once lubricated, makes manual labour easier.
explanation.walkthrough: The grease is not literal: put 'grease' after the joint word and you get the stock phrase for vigorous scrubbing or labour.
explanation.definitionFit: The bend between upper arm and forearm is a hinge joint, and elbow grease means hard physical effort.

clue.text: Desires to have apprentice replace new young horses

indicators.note: to replace is to put one thing in another's place, swapping a letter

parts.note: yearnings are longings or desires
L is for learner, as on a learner driver's plate
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A stable owner who wants a trainee to take over looking after the colts.
explanation.walkthrough: In YEARNINGS the N for new gives way to the L for learner.
explanation.definitionFit: A yearling is a racehorse or other animal between one and two years old, so a juvenile foal or colt.

clue.text: Dealer made to return revolutionary painting?

indicators.note: something made to go back retraces its path, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: red is the colour of revolutionary communism
painting is a form of art

explanation.surface: An art dealer forced to give back a radical canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dealer' sits naturally beside 'painting' as an art dealer, but it is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer buys and sells goods for profit, which is exactly what a trader does.

clue.text: In parts of Ottawa, shops are inundated

indicators.note: the letters needed lie inside portions of neighbouring words, spanning the gap

parts.note: the tail of the city and the start of the stores run together

explanation.surface: A flood in Canada's capital leaves shops under water.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma between the two words is ignored; the letters run across it.
explanation.definitionFit: Awash means covered or flooded with water, so a place awash is flooded or swamped.

clue.text: Semi-verbal, say, after drinking too much of this?

definitions.text: Semi-verbal, say, after drinking too much of this?

indicators.note: semi means half, so only half the word survives and the rest is cut

parts.note: a deletion keeps only the first half of the word, three of its six letters
to mouth is to say or utter words

explanation.surface: Someone who overdid a drink and can now barely speak.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: half-articulate speech is what too much of this drink would leave you with.
explanation.definitionFit: Vermouth is a fortified wine flavoured with herbs, a classic aperitif and cocktail ingredient that slurs speech if overdone.

clue.text: Without hesitation, the smallest note

indicators.note: without means lacking, so some letters are taken away

parts.note: the minimum is the smallest amount
um is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: A musician confidently naming the shortest note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The smallest note' looks like one definition, but a minim is far from the shortest note: it lasts two beats.
explanation.definitionFit: A minim is the British name for a half note in music, held for half the length of a semibreve.

clue.text: Bird will resist eating nuts, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, pointing to the opening letter of each word

parts.note: the first letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A small bird holding out against a meal of nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word between the definition and the indicator contributes its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The wren is a tiny brown songbird common in British gardens, with a short upright tail.

clue.text: Jail sentence still active after death — that's disproportionate

parts.words: Jail sentence still active after death
parts.note: surface reading: a prison term that outlasts the prisoner
setter's reading: a term longer than a life sentence would literally exceed one, which is the idiom for exaggerated

explanation.surface: A judge handing down a punishment so long it outlives the convict, which seems excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: A life sentence is the longest jail term; one that runs past death is bigger than it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something larger-than-life is exaggerated, flamboyant or out of normal scale, beyond ordinary proportions.

clue.text: One following whiskey carrier in this detective story

indicators.note: what follows comes behind, placing one piece after the others

parts.note: Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a hod is a builder's trough for carrying bricks
a unit is a single thing, one

explanation.surface: A mystery novel in which someone trails a bootlegger carrying whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' comes first in the clue but last in the answer, because it follows the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A whodunit is a crime novel or film centred on working out the culprit, from the phrase who done it.

clue.text: Star I'm backing to take off?

definitions.note: minus is a preposition meaning less; the phrase is a verb

indicators.note: to back is to go in reverse, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the Sun is our nearest star
taken as written

explanation.surface: A celebrity announcing they will support a plan to escape or fly away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' suggests departure, but here it is arithmetic: subtracting.
explanation.definitionFit: In arithmetic minus signals subtraction, deducting one number from another, which is taking it away.
